items.section: 0 Start here: Exact vs. approximate answers, and calculators
items.statement: “Extraneous” values in this unit show up as lost restrictions. When you simplify a composition, a cancelled factor or a squared root can hide an x that was never allowed. That’s why every domain here is found before simplifying, and why square-root inverses carry a restriction (Section 4).
I Can (Day 1): evaluate a function given a graph; add, subtract, multiply and divide two functions and simplify; find the domain of the result from an equation or a graph.
Domain of f + g, f − g, fg: D_f ∩ D_g, the x-values that are in both domains.
Domain of f/g: D_f ∩ D_g, and remove every x where g(x) = 0. (For g/f, remove the zeros of f.)
Find the domain before you simplify. Cancelling a factor does not bring back an x that was excluded.
Evaluating from a graph: f(a) is the y-value of the graph at x = a. So (f + g)(a) = f(a) + g(a): read both heights, then combine.
(fg)(x) means multiply. It is not the composition f(g(x)).

To compute (f + g)(a) you must compute f(a) and g(a) separately, so a has to be allowed by both functions. That’s the intersection. For f/g there is one more requirement, since you can’t divide by 0. Simplifying afterward doesn’t change what the original instructions required: if f(0) doesn’t exist, then (g/f)(0) doesn’t exist, even when the simplified formula would give a number at 0.

items.section: 1 How to recognize it & choose a method
items.statement: Domain written in words (“f has domain [−4, 9] and f(x) = 0 only at...”) → same steps on a number line.

Introductory Example 1.1  f(x) = sqrt(x + 3), g(x) = x − 1. Find f + g, fg, f/g, g/f and each domain. Domains first. sqrt(x + 3) needs x + 3 ≥ 0, so D_f = [−3, ∞). g is a line: D_g = ℝ. D_f ∩ D_g = [−3, ∞). Sum and product. (f + g)(x) = sqrt(x + 3) + x − 1 and (fg)(x) = (x − 1)sqrt(x + 3). Both have domain [−3, ∞). f/g. (f/g)(x) = sqrt(x + 3)/(x − 1). Remove g(x) = 0: x − 1 = 0 ⇒ x = 1. Domain [−3, 1) ∪ (1, ∞). g/f. (g/f)(x) = (x − 1)/sqrt(x + 3). Now f is on the bottom: f(x) = 0 when x = −3. Domain (−3, ∞). The endpoint −3 is gone. [continues onto page 6]
items.asked: Find f + g, fg, f/g, g/f and each domain.
items.official_answer: (f + g)(x) = sqrt(x + 3) + x − 1, domain [−3, ∞) (boxed); (fg)(x) = (x − 1)sqrt(x + 3), domain [−3, ∞) (boxed, shared with f+g); (f/g)(x) = sqrt(x + 3)/(x − 1), domain [−3, 1) ∪ (1, ∞) (boxed); (g/f)(x) = (x − 1)/sqrt(x + 3), domain (−3, ∞) (boxed)

items.statement: Test-level Example 1.2  f(x) = (x − 3)/x^2, g(x) = (x + 2)/(4 − x) (like Review #4). Find the domains of (f/g)(x) and (g/f)(x). 1. Restrictions of each function. f: x^2 ≠ 0 ⇒ x ≠ 0. g: 4 − x ≠ 0 ⇒ x ≠ 4. 2. Zeros of each function (a fraction is 0 when its numerator is 0): f(x) = 0 ⇒ x = 3; g(x) = 0 ⇒ x = −2. 3. f/g: exclude f’s and g’s restrictions and the zero of the denominator g: (f/g)(x) = (x − 3)/x^2 ÷ (x + 2)/(4 − x) = (x − 3)/x^2 · (4 − x)/(x + 2) = (x − 3)(4 − x)/(x^2(x + 2))   D_f/g: ℝ, x ≠ −2, 0, 4. Notice x = 4 is excluded even though 4 − x ends up on top. It came from g. 4. g/f: exclude 0, 4, and the zero of the denominator f (x = 3): (g/f)(x) = (x + 2)/(4 − x) · x^2/(x − 3) = x^2(x + 2)/((4 − x)(x − 3))   D_g/f: ℝ, x ≠ 0, 3, 4. The simplified form gives 0 at x = 0, but f(0) does not exist, so x = 0 stays excluded.
items.given: f(x) = (x − 3)/x^2; g(x) = (x + 2)/(4 − x). Restrictions: f: x ≠ 0; g: x ≠ 4. Zeros: f(x) = 0 ⇒ x = 3; g(x) = 0 ⇒ x = −2.

items.statement: I Can (Day 2): compose two functions and simplify; find the domain of a composition from an equation or a graph.

(f o g)(x) = f(g(x))   "f of g of x": x --g--> g(x) --f--> f(g(x)). (1) The function written closest to x acts first. Usually f(g(x)) != g(f(x)). (2) To simplify: replace every x in the outer rule with the whole inner rule, in parentheses. If you get a fraction inside a fraction, multiply the top and bottom by the LCD of the little fractions (your teacher writes . (x+5)/(x+5)). (3) Domain of f o g: x must be in D_g and the output g(x) must be in D_f. (4) Decide the domain before simplifying. The simplified formula can look defined at values that were never allowed.

items.section: 2 Composition & its domain - Why it works
items.statement: An input travels through g first, so g must accept it. Then g's output becomes f's input, so f must accept that. Example: in A(B(x)) with A(x) = (x+2)/(x-4), the number 4 is forbidden as an input to A. So any x that makes B(x) = 4 must be thrown out, even though B itself is fine there.

items.section: 2 Composition & its domain - How to recognize it & choose a method
items.statement: (1) f(g(2)) with numbers or graphs -> work inside-out: find g(2), then plug that into f. (2) "Find A(B(x)) and simplify" with fractions -> substitute, then multiply top and bottom by the LCD. (3) "Domain of f(g(x))" -> two checks: (1) x in D_g; (2) solve for the x's that make g(x) a bad input for f (a value that makes f's denominator 0, or makes f's radicand negative). (4) Outer function is sqrt and the inner one is a graph -> keep the x's where the graph is on or above the x-axis.

Example 2.1 f(x) = x^2 - 1, g(x) = 3x + 2. f(g(x)): put (3x + 2) in for x in f: f(3x + 2) = (3x + 2)^2 - 1 = 9x^2 + 12x + 4 - 1 = [9x^2 + 12x + 3]. g(f(x)): put (x^2 - 1) in for x in g: g(x^2 - 1) = 3(x^2 - 1) + 2 = [3x^2 - 1]. Different from f(g(x)). Check with a number. (f o g)(1) = f(g(1)) = f(5) = 24, and the formula gives 9 + 12 + 3 = 24. (check) Both domains are R (no fractions or roots).
items.official_answer: f(g(x)) = 9x^2 + 12x + 3; g(f(x)) = 3x^2 - 1; both domains R; check (f o g)(1) = 24

items.section: 2 Composition & its domain - Test-level Example 2.3 (like Day 12)
items.statement: Example 2.3 A(x) = (x+3)/(x-2), B(x) = 4/(x+1) (like Day 12). Find simplified A(B(x)) and its domain, then B(A(x)) and its domain. 1. Substitute. Replace each x in A with 4/(x+1): A(B(x)) = (4/(x+1) + 3)/(4/(x+1) - 2). 2. Clear the little fractions: multiply top and bottom by (x + 1) and distribute to every term: = (4/(x+1).(x+1) + 3(x+1))/(4/(x+1).(x+1) - 2(x+1)) = (4 + 3x + 3)/(4 - 2x - 2) = [(3x+7)/(2-2x)]. 3. Domain. From B: x != -1. From A: its input can't be 2, so solve B(x) = 2: 4/(x+1) = 2 => 4 = 2x + 2 => x = 1. D_{A o B}: [R, x != -1, 1]. The simplified denominator 2 - 2x shows only x != 1. The restriction x != -1 disappeared during simplifying, which is why you find the domain first. 4. The other order. B(A(x)) = 4/((x+3)/(x-2) + 1) . (x-2)/(x-2) = 4(x-2)/(x + 3 + (x-2)) = [(4x-8)/(2x+1)]. Domain: from A, x != 2. From B (input can't be -1): (x+3)/(x-2) = -1 => x + 3 = -x + 2 => x = -1/2. D_{B o A}: [R, x != 2, -1/2]. Check. x = 0: B(0) = 4, A(4) = 7/2; formula: (0+7)/(2-0) = 7/2. (check)

items.statement: I Can (Day 3): decompose a function into two functions that have been composed (pp. 13-16). Your test list says "no graphing" for this topic.

To decompose h(x) means to find an inner function g and an outer function f with h(x) = f(g(x)). (1) g = the inside chunk: what happens to x first. Look inside parentheses, under a radical, in a denominator, or in an exponent. (2) f = what is done to that chunk. Write f with x standing where the chunk was. (3) Neither f nor g may be just x. (g(x) = x, f = h is technically a composition but says nothing.) (4) Most functions decompose in more than one correct way. Your Day 12 warm-up asked for two.

Decomposition is composition run backward. Think about how you'd evaluate h(2) on a calculator: the first thing you compute is g(2) and the rest is f. Any place you could "pause" in that calculation gives a valid split.

items.section: 3 Decomposition - How to recognize it & choose a method
items.statement: Words like "find f and g so that h(x) = f(g(x))" or "decompose." Method: (1) circle the chunk that gets computed first, which is g(x); (2) replace that chunk with x in h, which gives f(x); (3) check by composing back.
Example 3.1 h(x) = (5x - 1)^4. The first thing computed is 5x - 1, then it's raised to the 4th power. g(x) = 5x - 1, f(x) = x^4. Check: f(g(x)) = (5x - 1)^4 = h(x). (check)

Example 3.2 Two ways: h(x) = 3/sqrt(x^2 + 4). Way 1 (smallest inside chunk). g(x) = x^2 + 4, f(x) = 3/sqrt(x). Check: f(g(x)) = 3/sqrt(x^2 + 4). (check) Way 2 (bigger inside chunk). g(x) = sqrt(x^2 + 4), f(x) = 3/x. Check: f(g(x)) = 3/sqrt(x^2 + 4). (check) (A third split also works: g(x) = x^2, f(x) = 3/sqrt(x+4).)
items.official_answer: Way 1: g(x) = x^2 + 4, f(x) = 3/sqrt(x); Way 2: g(x) = sqrt(x^2 + 4), f(x) = 3/x; Third split: g(x) = x^2, f(x) = 3/sqrt(x+4)

I Can (Days 4–5): determine whether a function has an inverse that is also a function (HLT); find the inverse, including rational inverses; use composition to verify that two functions are inverses.
f^-1 undoes f: if f(a) = b, then f^-1(b) = a. Every point (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f^-1, so the graph of f^-1 is the reflection of f over the line y = x.
Domain and range swap: D_{f^-1} = R_f and R_{f^-1} = D_f.

One-to-one: each output comes from exactly one input ("x's and y's don't repeat"). A function is one-to-one exactly when it passes the horizontal line test (HLT), and then its inverse is also a function.
Even functions never pass the HLT, because f(-x) = f(x) means two inputs share an output.
Find the rule: write y = f(x) -> swap x and y -> solve for y -> write f^-1(x) = ...
Verify by composition, both ways: f(g(x)) = x and g(f(x)) = x. If either one fails, they are not inverses.
f^-1(x) is not 1/f(x). The -1 means "inverse function," not an exponent.

Swapping x and y is the algebra version of trading inputs for outputs. If a horizontal line hits the graph twice, two different x's give the same y. The "inverse" would then have to send that one y back to two x's, which a function can't do. Composition checks the definition directly: undoing what you did gets you back to x.
Three graphs with captions: (1) "y = x^2 - 2: fails the HLT"  (2) "y = (1/4)x^3: passes"  (3) "f and f^-1 mirror over y = x".

items.section: 4 Inverses / Example 4.4 (Test-level) Rational inverse, verified both ways (like Review #1)
items.statement: Example 4.4 Rational inverse, verified both ways: f(x) = (2x - 5)/(3x + 4) (like Review #1). a. Find the inverse. x = (2y - 5)/(3y + 4) (swap x and y); x(3y + 4) = 2y - 5 (multiply by the denominator); 3xy + 4x = 2y - 5 (distribute); 3xy - 2y = -4x - 5 (all y-terms left, the rest right); y(3x - 2) = -4x - 5 (factor out y); f^-1(x) = (-4x - 5)/(3x - 2) (or (4x + 5)/(2 - 3x)).

c. Verify f^-1(f(x)) = x. Multiply top and bottom by (3x + 4): f^-1(f(x)) = [-4((2x - 5)/(3x + 4)) - 5] / [3((2x - 5)/(3x + 4)) - 2] · (3x + 4)/(3x + 4) = [-4(2x - 5) - 5(3x + 4)] / [3(2x - 5) - 2(3x + 4)] = (-8x + 20 - 15x - 20)/(6x - 15 - 6x - 8) = -23x/-23 = x ✓. Both compositions give x, so they are inverses. (Bonus check: f has a horizontal asymptote at y = 2/3, and f^-1 is undefined at x = 2/3. Range of f = domain of f^-1.)
items.official_answer: f^-1(f(x)) = (-8x + 20 - 15x - 20)/(6x - 15 - 6x - 8) = -23x/-23 = x. Both compositions give x, so they are inverses. (f has HA y = 2/3; f^-1 undefined at x = 2/3.)

items.section: 4 Inverses / Example 4.5 (Test-level) Square root (like quiz review #10)
items.statement: Example 4.5 Square root: f(x) = 3sqrt(x - 1) + 2 (like quiz review #10). Range of f first. sqrt(x - 1) >= 0, so f(x) >= 2: R_f = [2, ∞) and D_f = [1, ∞). x = 3sqrt(y - 1) + 2 (swap); (x - 2)/3 = sqrt(y - 1) (isolate the root); ((x - 2)/3)^2 = y - 1 (square both sides); f^-1(x) = ((x - 2)/3)^2 + 1, x >= 2. Why "x >= 2"? Squaring can't tell (x - 2)/3 from its opposite. On its own, the formula ((x - 2)/3)^2 + 1 is a whole parabola (not one-to-one), and it gives values that f never produced. Keeping D_{f^-1} = R_f = [2, ∞) throws out those extra values. That's the "extraneous" issue for this unit. (The graph at the start of this section shows both halves.) Your quiz-review key writes f^-1(x) = ((x - 4)/7)^2 for 7sqrt(x) + 4; the matching restriction there is x >= 4.

items.section: 4 Inverses / Example 4.6 (Test-level) Fractional power (like quiz review #13)
items.statement: Example 4.6 Fractional power: f(x) = 2(x - 4)^(3/5) + 1 (like quiz review #13). x = 2(y - 4)^(3/5) + 1 (swap); (x - 1)/2 = (y - 4)^(3/5) (isolate the power); ((x - 1)/2)^(5/3) = y - 4 (raise both sides to the reciprocal power 5/3); f^-1(x) = ((x - 1)/2)^(5/3) + 4. Check: f(36) = 2(32)^(3/5) + 1 = 2(8) + 1 = 17, and f^-1(17) = 8^(5/3) + 4 = 32 + 4 = 36. ✓ (The exponent 3/5 has an odd denominator, so there's no domain restriction.)

items.section: 4 Inverses / Example 4.7 (Test-level) "Are they inverses?" when they're not
items.statement: Example 4.7 "Are they inverses?" when they're not: f(x) = 2/(x - 1), g(x) = (x + 2)/2. f(g(x)) = 2/((x + 2)/2 - 1) · 2/2 = 4/(x + 2 - 2) = 4/x ≠ x. One composition already fails, so f and g are not inverses. (Your teacher still writes out both on quiz review #8. Do that if the directions say "both ways.") The true inverse is x = 2/(y - 1) ⇒ y - 1 = 2/x ⇒ f^-1(x) = 2/x + 1 = (x + 2)/x.
items.official_answer: Not inverses: f(g(x)) = 4/x ≠ x. True inverse of f: f^-1(x) = 2/x + 1 = (x + 2)/x.

items.statement: I Can (Days 6-7): describe the transformations (dilations, reflections, translations) in a function rule; graph the transformed function; determine the order; determine the domain and range after a transformation.

Key idea: y = a f(b(x - h)) + k. Table columns: 'Outside f: acts on y (vertical)' | 'Inside f: acts on x (horizontal, "backwards")'. Row 'negative': a < 0: reflect over the x-axis | b < 0: reflect over the y-axis. Row 'size': |a| > 1: vertical stretch by |a|; 0 < |a| < 1: vertical compression by |a| | |b| > 1: horizontal compression by 1/|b|; 0 < |b| < 1: horizontal stretch by 1/|b|. Row 'shift': +k: up k; -k: down | (x - h): right h; (x + h): left h.
Factor b out of the inside first. f(4x - 8) = f(4(x - 2)): right 2. f(-x + 3) = f(-(x - 3)): reflect over the y-axis, right 3. f(1/3 x - 1) = f(1/3 (x - 3)): right 3.
items.official_answer: f(4(x - 2)): right 2; f(-(x - 3)): reflect over the y-axis, right 3; f(1/3 (x - 3)): right 3

items.statement: Proper order: reflections and dilations before translations. Your teacher lists them as: a (reflect over x-axis, vertical stretch/compression) -> b (reflect over y-axis, horizontal stretch/compression) -> h (left/right) -> k (up/down).
Mapping rule (a point (x, y) on f goes to): (x, y) -> (x/b + h, a y + k)
Domain and range: send the endpoints of D_f through x/b + h and the endpoints of R_f through ay + k. If b < 0 or a < 0 the endpoints come out reversed, so re-order them as [smaller, larger].

Why it works. Why the inside is "backwards." Say f(2) = 5. On h(x) = f(3(x - 1)), which x gives that same output 5? You need 3(x - 1) = 2, so x = 2/3 + 1. In general the old x0 moves to x = x0/b + h. You divide by b (so |b| > 1 squeezes) and you add h (so x - h moves right). Why order matters. Outside, a f(x) + k means "multiply, then add." So -f(x) + 3 is reflect, then up 3. But "up 3, then reflect" is -(f(x) + 3) = -f(x) - 3, a different graph. Inside, f(4(x - 2)) is compress, then right 2. Shifting first gives f(4x - 2) = f(4(x - 1/2)), which only moves right 1/2.

How to recognize it & choose a method. (1) "State the transformations in a proper order" -> rewrite in a f(b(x - h)) + k form (factor b), then list a, b, h, k. (2) "Graph h(x)" given a graph of f -> mapping table on every corner and endpoint, then connect the new points in the same order. (3) "f has domain ... and range ...; find the domain and range of h" -> endpoints only, no graph needed (Review #5, quiz #7). (4) "Write an equation for: horizontal compression by 1/4, shift right 2" -> build the inside as b(x - h); watch for the word THEN, which forces parentheses.

items.statement: I Can (Days 6-7): graph a function that involves an absolute value transformation; find its domain and range. Class notes pp. 30-34 (Days 8-9).

Key idea. Column y = |f(x)| (absolute value on the outputs, y): * Reflect every negative y-value over the x-axis. * Keep the positive y-values the same. * Mark and keep the x-intercepts; they become corners. * No points end up in Q3 or Q4. * Domain: unchanged. Range: if R_f = [c, d] with c < 0 < d, it becomes [0, max(|c|, d)]. Column y = f(|x|) (absolute value on the inputs, x): * Delete the part of the graph with x < 0. * Keep the right side (x >= 0) and reflect it over the y-axis. * The result always has even symmetry. * Domain: if D_f = [p, q] with p <= 0 < q, it becomes [-q, q]. * Range: whatever f reaches on x >= 0 (read it off the graph).

items.statement: Combining with other transformations (p. 32): "Apply the operations to each point in the order they would be applied if you were inputting an x-value." Inside work (x-shifts, |x|, b) comes first, then f, then the outside work in order: |y|, then multiply by a, then add k. Track the endpoints and the x- and y-intercepts.

Why it works. |f(x)| can't output a negative number, so anything below the x-axis flips up. Points with y = 0 stay put, which is why the x-intercepts become the hinge points. For f(|x|), the input -3 gets turned into 3 before f sees it, so the output at x = -3 copies the output at x = 3. The left half becomes a mirror image of the right half. That's even symmetry: j(-x) = f(|-x|) = f(|x|) = j(x), true for any f (Day 8 notes).

How to recognize it & choose a method. (1) Bars around f( ) or around the whole output -> |y|: flip negatives up. (2) Bars around x inside f -> f(|x|): delete the left side, mirror the right. (3) A shift before the bars, like |f(x) - 1| or |f(x - 5)| -> do that shift first, find the new x-intercepts, then flip. (4) "Domain of 2f(|x|) + 1" or "range of 2|f(x)| + 1" from D and R only -> use the rules in the table, then apply a and k (Review #3A-B).

I Can (Days 8–9): identify the coefficient and exponent of a power function; sketch its graph from them. Class notes pp. 35–44 (Days 10–11).

Key idea. Power function: f(x) = k x^p, with k ≠ 0 (the coefficient) and p ≠ 0 (the power). p can be a whole number, a fraction, or negative. Write p = a/b in lowest terms.
► Not power functions: y = 2 (constant function, a horizontal line); y = e^x (exponential: the variable is in the exponent).
► Shape in Q1 (take k > 0): p > 1 ("higher/lower" fraction): increasing, curves up (concave up). 0 < p < 1 ("lower/higher"): increasing, curves down (concave down). p < 0: decreasing toward the x-axis, with asymptotes x = 0 and y = 0. Every graph passes through (1, k).
► Numerator a = symmetry, denominator b = root:
   ► b even (an even root): Q1 only, so f is undefined for x < 0. Domain [0, ∞), or (0, ∞) if p < 0.
   ► b odd and a even: even symmetry, so the graph is in Q1 and Q2.
   ► b odd and a odd: odd symmetry, so the graph is in Q1 and Q3.
► k < 0 reflects over the x-axis: Q1→Q4, Q2→Q3, Q3→Q2. A bigger |k| makes the graph steeper.

items.statement: Why it works. x^(a/b) = (nthroot(b, x))^a. The denominator is a root. An even root of a negative number isn't real, so b even leaves no graph for x < 0. An odd root of a negative number is real, so the left side exists. The numerator is a power applied to that root: an even power erases the sign (left side copies the right, even symmetry), and an odd power keeps it (left side is the right side turned upside down, odd symmetry). For the Q1 shape, compare with y = x: for p > 1 the graph is below y = x on (0, 1) and above it after x = 1 (curves up); for 0 < p < 1 it's the reverse; for p < 0, x^p = 1/x^|p| blows up near 0 and shrinks toward 0 for large x.

How to recognize it & choose a method.
► "Identify k and p" or "write in the form y = kx^a" → rewrite radicals as fractional exponents and move x out of the denominator with a negative exponent: nthroot(n, x^m) = x^(m/n), 1/x^n = x^(-n), sqrt(4x^3) = sqrt(4) sqrt(x^3) = 2x^(3/2).
► "Even, odd, or undefined for x < 0?" → reduce p = a/b and look at the parities of a and b.
► "Describe the portion in Q1 or Q4" → sign of k picks Q1 or Q4; size of p picks the shape.
► "Describe the attributes" → domain, range, continuity, increasing, decreasing, boundedness, asymptotes, end behavior.
► "Write an equation for this graph" (rational, non-integer power) → quadrants give the parities, the Q1 shape gives the size of p, and a flip gives k < 0.
